newsitem.title: BRAZIL: "No problems" between Brazil and Argentina - Malan.
newsitem.headline: "No problems" between Brazil and Argentina - Malan.

text.p: Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan denied any conflict between Brazil and Argentina or Brazil and its partners in the Mercosur customs union.

Speaking at a news conference, in which he was accompanied by Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez, Malan blasted reports of friction among the partners of the South American free trade agreement.
"There is no problem between Brazil and Argentina or between Brazil and Mercosur," Malan said.

Malan said the two countries had agreed to make an exemption for Mercosur imports up to a value of $40,000 if they were backed by guarantees from their respective Central Banks using so-called CCR (Reciprocal Trade Credits) contracts.
Malan said Brazil had changed the definition of paying "in cash" for imports from Mercosur countries, effectively lengthening the time importers have to pay for imported goods.

Malan said that previously the definition of "paying in cash" meant paying for the goods the month after the taking out a foreign exchange contract on the deal. The definition would now be two months after, he said.
Malan said the Brazilian Central Bank would hold a news conference either later today or on Thursday in which it would offer more details about the measures that were agreed upon in today's meeting.
The meeting between Malan and Fernandez was called after the two countries clashed publicly after Brazil announced new restrictions on financing rules last week.
The new rules, which were announced without consulting Brazil's Mercosur partners, triggered a wave of protest from government, the press and business circles in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.

At the news conference, Malan acknowleged that he and the Brazilian Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia should have at least informed their Mercosur counterparts that these measures were being considered.
"We did not explain with the necessary detail the reasons that led us to take these decisions," Malan told reporters.
However, he stressed that the financing restrictions were of a macroeconomic nature and not commercial, and that they should not be interpreted in any way as protectionist.
